name: Credentials In Files
description:
Adversaries may search local file systems and remote file shares for files containing insecurely stored credentials. These can be files created by users to store their own credentials, shared credential stores for a group of individuals, configuration files containing passwords for a system or service, or source code/binary files containing embedded passwords.

It is possible to extract passwords from backups or saved virtual machines through [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003).(Citation: CG 2014) Passwords may also be obtained from Group Policy Preferences stored on the Windows Domain Controller.(Citation: SRD GPP)

In cloud and/or containerized environments, authenticated user and service account credentials are often stored in local configuration and credential files.(Citation: Unit 42 Hildegard Malware) They may also be found as parameters to deployment commands in container logs.(Citation: Unit 42 Unsecured Docker Daemons) In some cases, these files can be copied and reused on another machine or the contents can be read and then used to authenticate without needing to copy any files.(Citation: Specter Ops - Cloud Credential Storage)

telemetry.name: Command Execution
telemetry.description: Execution of a command and its interpreter or parent context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect process command lines and relevant shell/interpreter audit; shell history alone is neither complete nor tamper-resistant.

providers.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
providers.scope: Script content via event 4104 when configured; channel depends on PowerShell edition.

providers.name: Sysmon process events
providers.scope: Interpreter launch and parent context, not full script content.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: execve-family execution context; shell built-ins need additional instrumentation.

configuration: Enable Script Block Logging through the policy/configuration for the installed edition. Forward Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for Windows PowerShell, or PowerShellCore/Operational for PowerShell 7.
Retain script-block ID and fragment ordering alongside process creation. Protect access to collected script text; secrets may be included.
On Linux, use narrowly scoped Audit execution rules for the lab account and supported architectures, and retain joined SYSCALL/EXECVE/PATH records.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Script content and process command lines are different signals. Logging may be partial, fragmented, filtered or disabled; never assume a command line reveals everything executed.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per host role and principal: rare interpreters, command argument patterns and parent-child sequences. Normalize scripts carefully; obfuscation, administrative automation and missing command lines change visibility.

telemetry.name: File Access
telemetry.description: Access to file objects with user, process and access-right context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Enable Audit File System plus a narrow SACL on a lab directory; on Linux select path/syscall rules and join associated Audit records.

providers.name: Windows Security auditing
providers.scope: Policy-dependent account, object, task and logon records on the host that performs the operation.

configuration: Use a lab-only GPO under Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration. Enable the specific subcategory named below.
For object-level auditing, configure a narrow system access control list (SACL) on the test object in addition to policy. Do not audit an entire production directory by default.

Forward Security events from the responsible host or controller; retain subject and target identities, object identifiers, result and original XML. Confirm effective policy with auditpol /get /category:*.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: A policy checkbox alone does not guarantee an event. Host role, SACL, success/failure selection and audit policy precedence matter. Directory changes may arrive as multiple records.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per principal, host and object: unusual access/request rates, new principal-object relationships, and changes outside approved administration windows. Control for service accounts and scheduled directory maintenance.

telemetry.name: File Creation
telemetry.description: Creation or overwrite of a file at an observed path.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon FileCreate (11) to the lab directory; retain the process and file path. Differentiate creation/overwrite if the sensor can.

providers.scope: Windows event-based collection; enable the event types needed below.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: Linux alternative for supported system-call and file events; different semantics and fields.

providers.name: Apple Endpoint Security clients
providers.scope: macOS alternative where the subscribed event exists; requires an entitled, approved client, not an iOS collector.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.

telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.

strategies.name: Detect Access to Unsecured Credential Files Across Platforms

analytics.name: Analytic 0856
analytics.guidance: Correlated file access to insecure credential files (e.g., *.env, *.xml, *.ps1) followed by suspicious process execution or authentication using retrieved credentials. Detected through Sysmon logs and Windows Security Event logs.

tuning.description: Patterns like *.env, *credential* can be tuned to reduce noise or catch custom implementations
Defines scope of access (e.g., only untrusted parent processes or high-risk processes)
Time delta between credential file access and use in logon attempt

analytics.name: Analytic 0857
analytics.guidance: File reads or process executions involving insecurely stored credential files (e.g., config files with password fields) by non-root or anomalous users followed by ssh authentication attempts.

tuning.description: Patterns like password, secret, token can be expanded or customized
Scope of users monitored (e.g., root vs all users)
Time between suspicious file access and credential use

log_sources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
log_sources.channel: open/read of sensitive config or secret files

log_sources.name: auditd:EXECVE
log_sources.channel: grep/cat/awk on files with password fields

analytics.name: Analytic 0858
analytics.guidance: Terminal-based grep or open of plist/config files containing credentials, correlated with Keychain or system login attempts.

tuning.description: Monitor unexpected use of security CLI or Keychain helper binaries
Add or remove watched file types based on system usage

log_sources.name: macos:unifiedlog
log_sources.channel: grep/cat on files matching credential patterns

analytics.name: Analytic 0859
analytics.guidance: Container processes accessing mounted secrets or configuration paths (e.g., /run/secrets, /mnt/config) followed by network access or credential use.

tuning.description: Tune anomaly scoring for container image deviations

log_sources.name: kubernetes:audit
log_sources.channel: process execution involving curl, grep, or awk on secrets

log_sources.name: cni:netflow
log_sources.channel: outbound connection to internal or external APIs

analytics.name: Analytic 0860
analytics.guidance: Access to local credential/config files (e.g., ~/.aws/credentials) followed by metadata API calls or cloud role assumptions.

tuning.description: Regex to match common credential files (e.g., *.aws/credentials, token.txt)
Adjust scope of roles monitored (e.g., admin, service accounts)
Correlation timing between file access and AssumeRole

log_sources.name: CloudTrail:GetObject
log_sources.channel: sensitive credential files in buckets or local image storage

log_sources.name: AWS:CloudTrail
log_sources.channel: sudden role assumption after credential file access

software.name: pngdowner
software.description: If an initial connectivity check fails, [pngdowner](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0067) attempts to extract proxy details and credentials from Windows Protected Storage and from the IE Credentials Store. This allows the adversary to use the proxy credentials for subsequent requests if they enable outbound HTTP access.(Citation: CrowdStrike Putter Panda)

mitigations.name: User Training
mitigations.description: Ensure that developers and system administrators are aware of the risk associated with having plaintext passwords in software configuration files that may be left on endpoint systems or servers.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.description: Restrict file shares to specific directories with access only to necessary users.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.description: Establish an organizational policy that prohibits password storage in files.

mitigations.name: Audit
mitigations.description: Preemptively search for files containing passwords and take actions to reduce the exposure risk when found.
